entries.35faa1c6c2481648d77d267e45285b97d21a8b95: <div sID="gen5833" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="26" osisID="1Sam.26" sID="1Sam.26"/> <div eID="gen5833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5834" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> David's troubles from Saul here begin again; and the clouds return after the rain, when one would have hoped the storm had blown over, and the sky had cleared upon that side; but after Saul had owned his fault in persecuting David, and acknowledged David's title to the crown, yet here he revives the persecution, so perfectly lost was he to all sense of honour and virtue. I. The Ziphites informed him where David was (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">ver. 1</reference>), and thereupon he marched out with a considerable force in quest of him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.2-1Sam.26.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. II. David gained intelligence of his motions (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.4">ver. 4</reference>), and took a view of his camp, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. He and one of his men ventured into his camp in the night and found him and all his guards fast asleep, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.6-1Sam.26.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. David, though much urged to it by his companions, would not take away Saul's life, but only carried off his spear and his cruse of water, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8-1Sam.26.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. V. He produced these as a further witness for him that he did not design any ill to Saul, and reasoned with him upon his conduct, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.13-1Sam.26.20">ver. 13-20</reference>. VI. Saul was hereby convinced of his error, and once more desisted from persecuting David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.21-1Sam.26.25">ver. 21-25</reference>. The story is much like that which we had (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1-1Sam.24.22">ch. xxiv.</reference>). In both David is delivered out of Saul's hand, and Saul out of David's.
entries.7a97e8918b3b9436ab86e0bee3875294a6718ac6: <div eID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5834" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Again Pursues David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1056.)</title> <div sID="gen5836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> before Jeshimon? <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Saul arose, and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, having three thousand chosen men of Israel with him, to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Saul pitched in the hill of Hachilah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Jeshimon, by the way. But David abode in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness. <hi type="super">4</hi> David therefore sent out spies, and understood that Saul was come in very deed. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David arose, and came to the place where Saul had pitched: and David beheld the place where Saul lay, and Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host: and Saul lay in the trench, and the people pitched round about him. <div eID="gen5836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5837" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Saul gets information of David's movements and acts offensively. The Ziphites came to him and told him where David now was, in the same place where he was when they formerly betrayed him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">ch. xxiii. 19</reference>. Perhaps (though it is not mentioned) Saul had given them intimation, under-hand, that he continued his design against David, and would be glad of their assistance. If not, they were very officious to Saul, aware of what would please him, and very malicious against David, to whom they despaired of ever reconciling themselves, and therefore they stirred up Saul (who needed no such spur) against him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">v. 1</reference>. For aught we know, Saul would have continued in the same good mind that he was in (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.17">ch. xxiv. 17</reference>), and would not have given David this fresh trouble, if the Ziphites had not put him on. See what need we have to pray to God that, since we have so much of the tinder of corruption in our own hearts, the sparks of temptation may be kept far from us, lest, if they come together, we be set on fire of hell. Saul readily caught at the information, and went down with an army of 3000 men to the place where David hid himself, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.2">v. 2</reference>. How soon do unsanctified hearts lose the good impressions which their convictions have made upon them and return with the dog to their vomit! <div eID="gen5837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5838" type="x-p"/> 2. David gets information of Saul's movements and acts defensively. He did not march out to meet and fight him; he sought only his own safety, not Saul's ruin; therefore he <hi type="italic">abode in the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.3">v. 3</reference>), putting thereby a great force upon himself, and curbing the bravery of his own spirit by a silent retirement, showing more true valour than he could have done by an irregular resistance. (1.) He had spies who informed him of Saul's descent, <hi type="italic">that he had come in very deed</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.4">v. 4</reference>); for he would not believe that Saul would deal so basely with him till he had the utmost evidence of it. (2.) He observed with his own eyes how Saul was encamped, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.5">v. 5</reference>. He came towards the place where Saul and his men had pitched their tents, so near as to be able, undiscovered, to take a view of their entrenchments, probably in the dusk of the evening.
entries.f9c3992e892719a2dc50c56867a59c9c5af8d7fa: <div eID="gen5838" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Spares Saul's Life. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1056.)</title> <div sID="gen5839" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Then answered David and said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Abishai the son of Zeruiah, brother to Joab, saying, Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp? And Abishai said, I will go down with thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> So David and Abishai came to the people by night: and, behold, Saul lay sleeping within the trench, and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster: but Abner and the people lay round about him. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then said Abishai to David, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day: now therefore let me smite him, I pray thee, with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not <hi type="italic">smite</hi> him the second time. <hi type="super">9</hi> And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed, and be guiltless? <hi type="super">10</hi> David said furthermore, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed: but, I pray thee, take thou now the spear that <hi type="italic">is</hi> at his bolster, and the cruse of water, and let us go. <hi type="super">12</hi> So David took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster; and they gat them away, and no man saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> nor knew <hi type="italic">it,</hi> neither awaked: for they <hi type="italic">were</hi> all asleep; because a deep sleep from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was fallen upon them. <div eID="gen5839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5840" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. David's bold adventure into Saul's camp in the night, accompanied only by his kinsman Abishai, the son of Zeruiah. He proposed it to him and to another of his confidants (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.6">v. 6</reference>), but the other either declined it as too dangerous an enterprise, or at least was content that Abishai, who was forward to it, should run the risk of it rather than himself. Whether David was prompted to do this by his own courage, or by an extraordinary impression upon his spirits, or by the oracle, does not appear; but, like Gideon, he ventured through the guards, with a special assurance of the divine protection. <div eID="gen5840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5841" type="x-p"/> II. The posture he found the camp in <hi type="italic">Saul lay sleeping in the trench,</hi> or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">in his chariot, and in the midst of his carriages,</hi> with <hi type="italic">his spear stuck in the ground</hi> by him, to be ready if his quarters should by beaten up (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.7">v. 7</reference>); and all the soldiers, even those that were appointed to stand sentinel, were <hi type="italic">fast asleep,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.12">v. 12</reference>. Thus were their eyes closed and their hands bound, <hi type="italic">for a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them;</hi> something extraordinary there was in it that they should all be asleep together, and so fast asleep that David and Abishai walked and talked among them, and yet none of them stirred. Sleep, when God gives it to his beloved, is their rest and refreshment; but he can, when he pleases, make it to his enemies their imprisonment. Thus are the <hi type="italic">stout-hearted spoiled; they have slept their sleep, and none of the men of might have found their hands, at thy rebuke, O God of Jacob!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5-Ps.76.6">Ps. lxxvi. 5, 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">It was a deep sleep from the Lord,</hi> who has the command of the powers of nature, and makes them to serve his purposes as he pleases. Whom God will disable, or destroy, he binds up with <hi type="italic">a spirit of slumber,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 8</reference>. How helpless do Saul and all his forces lie, all, in effect, disarmed and chained! and yet nothing is done to them; they are only rocked asleep. How easily can God weaken the strongest, befool the wisest, and baffle the most watchful! Let all his friends therefore trust him and all his enemies fear him. <div eID="gen5841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5842" type="x-p"/> III. Abishai's request to David for a commission to dispatch Saul with the spear that stuck at his bolster, which (now that he lay so fair) he undertook to do at one blow, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">v. 8</reference>. He would not urge David to kill him himself, because he had declined doing this before when he had a similar opportunity; but he begged earnestly that David would give him leave to do it, pleading that he was his enemy, not only cruel and implacable, but false and perfidious, whom no reason would rule nor kindness work upon, and that <hi type="italic">God had now delivered him into his hand,</hi> and did in effect bid him strike. The last advantage he had of this kind was indeed but accidental, when Saul happened to be in the cave with him at the same time. But in this there was something extraordinary; the deep sleep that had fallen on Saul and all his guards was manifestly from the Lord, so that it was a special providence which gave him this opportunity; he ought not therefore to let it slip. <div eID="gen5842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5843" type="x-p"/> IV. David's generous refusal to suffer any harm to be done to Saul, and in it a resolute adherence to his principles of loyalty, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.9">v. 9</reference>. David charged Abishai not to destroy him, would not only not do it himself, but not permit another to do it. And he gave two reasons for it:—1. It would be a sinful affront to God's ordinance. Saul was the Lord's anointed, king of Israel by the special appointment and nomination of the God of Israel, the power that was, and to resist him was to <hi type="italic">resist the ordinance of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.2">Rom. xiii. 2</reference>. No man could do it and be guiltless. The thing he feared was guilt and his concern respected his innocence more than his safety. 2. It would be a sinful anticipation of God's providence. God had sufficiently shown him, in Nabal's case, that, if he left it to him to avenge him, he would do it in due time. Encouraged therefore by his experience in that instance, he resolves to wait till God shall think fit to avenge him on Saul, and he will by no means <hi type="italic">avenge himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">"The Lord shall smite him,</hi> as he did Nabal, with some sudden stroke, or he shall <hi type="italic">die in battle</hi> (as it proved he did soon after), or, if not, <hi type="italic">his day shall come to die</hi> a natural death, and I will contentedly wait till then, rather than force my way to the promised crown by any indirect methods." The temptation indeed was very strong; but, if he should yield, he would sin against God, and therefore he will resist the temptation with the utmost resolution (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord forbid that I should stretch forth my hand against the Lord's anointed;</hi> no, I will never do it, nor suffer it to be done." Thus bravely does he prefer his conscience to his interest and trusts God with the issue. <div eID="gen5843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5844" type="x-p"/> V. The improvement he made of this opportunity for the further evidence of his own integrity. He and Abishai carried away the spear and cruse of water which Saul had by his bed-side (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.12">v. 12</reference>), and, which was very strange, none of all the guards were aware of it. If a physician had given them the strongest opiate or stupifying dose, they could not have been faster locked up with sleep. Saul's spear which he had by him for defence, and his cup of water which he had for his refreshment, were both stolen from him while he slept. Thus do we lose our strength and our comfort when we are careless, and secure, and off our watch.
entries.2fbc1d644e54abb29d7ef29d047427f9c2fb1378: <div eID="gen5844" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Expostulates with Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1056.)</title> <div sID="gen5845" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Then David went over to the other side, and stood on the top of a hill afar off; a great space <hi type="italic">being</hi> between them: <hi type="super">14</hi> And David cried to the people, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, Answerest thou not, Abner? Then Abner answered and said, Who <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou <hi type="italic">that</hi> criest to the king? <hi type="super">15</hi> And David said to Abner, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> not thou a <hi type="italic">valiant</hi> man? and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> like to thee in Israel? wherefore then hast thou not kept thy lord the king? for there came one of the people in to destroy the king thy lord. <hi type="super">16</hi> This thing <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good that thou hast done. <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> worthy to die, because ye have not kept your master, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed. And now see where the king's spear <hi type="italic">is,</hi> and the cruse of water that <hi type="italic">was</hi> at his bolster. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Saul knew David's voice, and said, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> this thy voice, my son David? And David said, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> my voice, my lord, O king. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he said, Wherefore doth my lord thus pursue after his servant? for what have I done? or what evil <hi type="italic">is</hi> in mine hand? <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore, I pray thee, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have stirred thee up against me, let him accept an offering: but if <hi type="italic">they be</hi> the children of men, cursed <hi type="italic">be</hi> they before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for they have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Go, serve other gods. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains. <div eID="gen5845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5846" type="x-p"/> David having got safely from Saul's camp himself, and having brought with him proofs sufficient that he had been there, posts himself conveniently, so that they might hear him and yet not reach him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.13">v. 13</reference>), and then begins to reason with them upon what had passed. <div eID="gen5846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5847" type="x-p"/> I. He reasons ironically with Abner, and keenly banters him. David knew well that it was from the mighty power of God that Abner and the rest of the guards were cast into so deep a sleep, and that God's immediate hand was in it; but he reproaches Abner as unworthy to be captain of the lifeguards, since he could sleep when the king his master lay so much exposed. By this it appears that the hand of God locked them up in this deep sleep that, as soon as ever David had got out of danger, a very little thing awakened them, even David's voice at a great distance roused them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.14">v. 14</reference>. Abner got up (we may suppose it early in a summer's morning) and enquired who called, and disturbed the king's repose. "It is I," says David, and then he upbraids him with his sleeping when he should have been upon his guard. Perhaps Abner, looking upon David as a despicable enemy and one that there was no danger from, had neglected to set a watch; however, he himself ought to have been more wakeful. David, to put him into confusion, told him, 1. That he had lost his honour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Art not thou a man?</hi> (so the word is), a man in office, that art bound, by the duty of thy place, to inspect the soldiery? Art not thou in reputation for a valiant man? So thou wouldst be esteemed, a man of such courage and conduct that there is none like thee; but now thou art shamed for ever. Thou a general! Thou, a sluggard!" 2. That he deserved to lose his head (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You are all worthy to die,</hi> by martial law, for being off your guard, when you had the king himself asleep in the midst of you. <hi type="italic">Ecce signum—Behold this token.</hi> See where the king's spear is, in the hand of him whom the king himself is pleased to count his enemy. Those that took away this might as easily and safely have taken away his life. Now see who are the king's best friends, you that neglected him and left him exposed or I that protected him when he was exposed. You pursue me as worthy to die, and irritate Saul against me; but who is worthy to die now?" Note, Sometimes those that unjustly condemn others are justly left to fall into condemnation themselves. <div eID="gen5847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5848" type="x-p"/> II. He reasons seriously and affectionately with Saul. By this time he was so well awake as to hear what was said, and to discern who said it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is this thy voice, my son David?</hi> In the same manner he had expressed his relentings, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.16">ch. xxiv. 16</reference>. He had given his wife to another and yet calls him <hi type="italic">son,</hi> thirsted after his blood and yet is glad to hear his voice. Those are bad indeed that have never any convictions of good, nor ever sincerely utter good expressions. And now David has as fair an opportunity of reaching Saul's conscience as he had just now of taking away his life. This he lays hold on, though not of that, and enters into a close argument with him, concerning the trouble he still continued to give him, endeavouring to persuade him to let fall the prosecution and be reconciled. <div eID="gen5848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> 1. He complains of the very melancholy condition he was brought into by the enmity of Saul against him. Two things he laments:—(1.) That he was driven from his master and from his business: "<hi type="italic">My lord pursues after his servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.18">v. 18</reference>. How gladly would I serve thee as formerly if my service might be accepted! but, instead of being owned as a servant, I am pursued as a rebel, and my lord is my enemy, and he whom I would follow with respect compels me to flee from him." (2.) That he was driven from his God and from his religion; and this was a much greater grievance than the former (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">v. 19</reference>): "They have <hi type="italic">driven me out from the inheritance of the Lord,</hi> have made Canaan too hot for me, at least the inhabited parts of it, have forced me into the deserts and mountains, and will, ere long, oblige me entirely to quit the country." And that which troubled him was not so much that he was driven out from his own inheritance as that he was driven out from the <hi type="italic">inheritance of the Lord,</hi> the holy land. It should be more comfortable to us to think of God's title to our estates and his interest in them than of our own, and that with them we may honour him than that with them we may maintain ourselves. Nor was it so much his trouble that he was constrained to live among strangers as that he was constrained to live among the worshippers of strange gods and was thereby thrust into temptation to join with them in their idolatrous worship. His enemies did, in effect, send him to <hi type="italic">go and serve other gods,</hi> and perhaps he had heard that some of them had spoken to that purport of him. Those that forbid our attendance on God's ordinances do what in them lies to estrange us from God and to make us heathens. If David had not been a man of extraordinary grace, and firmness to his religion, the ill usage he met with from his own prince and people, who were Israelites and worshippers of the true God, would have prejudiced him against the religion they professed and have driven him to communicate with idolaters. "If these be Israelites," he might have said, "let me live and die with Philistines;" and no thanks to them that their conduct had not that effect. We are to reckon that the greatest injury that can be done us which exposes us to sin. Of those who thus led David into temptation he here says, <hi type="italic">Cursed be they before the Lord.</hi> Those fall under a curse that thrust out those whom God receives, and send those to the devil who are dear to God. <div eID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5850" type="x-p"/> 2. He insists upon his own innocency: <hi type="italic">What have I done or what evil is in my hand?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.18">v. 18</reference>. He had the testimony of his conscience for him that he had never done nor ever designed any mischief to the person, honour, or government, of his prince, nor to any of the interests of his country. He had lately had Saul's own testimony concerning him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.17">ch. xxiv. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art more righteous than I.</hi> It was very unreasonable and wicked for Saul to pursue him as a criminal, when he could not charge him with any crime. <div eID="gen5850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5851" type="x-p"/> 3. He endeavours to convince Saul that his pursuit of him is not only wrong, but mean, and much below him: "<hi type="italic">The king of Israel,</hi> whose dignity is great, and who has so much other work to do, <hi type="italic">has come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">v. 20</reference>—a poor game for the king of Israel to pursue. He compares himself to a partridge, a very innocent harmless bird, which, when attempts are made upon its life, flies if it can, but makes no resistance. And would Saul bring the flower of his army into the field only to hunt one poor partridge? What a disparagement was this to his honour! What a stain would it be on his memory to trample upon so weak and patient as well as so innocent an enemy! <reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">James v. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">You have killed the just, and he doth not resist you.</hi> <div eID="gen5851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5852" type="x-p"/> 4. He desires that the core of the controversy may be searched into and some proper method taken to bring it to an end, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">v. 19</reference>. Saul himself could not say that justice put him on thus to persecute David, or that he was obliged to do it for the public safety. David was not willing to say (though it was very true) that Saul's own envy and malice put him on to do it; and therefore he concludes it must be attributed either to the righteous judgment of God or to the unrighteous designs of evil men. Now, (1.) "<hi type="italic">If the Lord have stirred thee up against me,</hi> either in displeasure to me (taking this way to punish me for my sins against him, though, as to thee, I am guiltless) or in displeasure to thee, if it be the effect of that evil spirit from the Lord which troubles thee, <hi type="italic">let him accept an offering</hi> from us both—let us join in making our peace with God, reconciling ourselves to him, which may be done, by sacrifice; and then I hope the sin will be pardoned, whatever it is, and the trouble, which is so great a vexation both to thee and me, will come to an end." See the right method of peace-making; let us first make God our friend by Christ the great Sacrifice, and then all other enmities shall be slain, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Eph. ii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.7">Prov. xvi. 7</reference>. But, (2.) "If thou art incited to it by wicked men, that incense thee against me, <hi type="italic">cursed be they before the Lord,</hi>" that is, they are very wicked people, and it is fit that they should be abandoned as such, and excluded from the king's court and councils. He decently lays the blame upon the evil counsellors who advised the king to that which was dishonourable and dishonest, and insists upon it that they be removed from about him and forbidden his presence, as men cursed before the Lord, and then he hoped he should gain his petition, which is (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">v. 20</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Let not my blood fall to the earth,</hi> as thou threatenest, for it is <hi type="italic">before the face of the Lord,</hi> who will take cognizance of the wrong and avenge it." Thus pathetically does David plead with Saul for his life, and, in order to that, for his favourable opinion of him.
entries.94e281892dc8e4990a76cb8c62325fdfa363cf36: <div eID="gen5852" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Relents. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1056.)</title> <div sID="gen5853" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Then said Saul, I have sinned: return, my son David: for I will no more do thee harm, because my soul was precious in thine eyes this day: behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly. <hi type="super">22</hi> And David answered and said, Behold the king's spear! and let one of the young men come over and fetch it. <hi type="super">23</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered thee into <hi type="italic">my</hi> hand to day, but I would not stretch forth mine hand against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed. <hi type="super">24</hi> And, behold, as thy life was much set by this day in mine eyes, so let my life be much set by in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and let him deliver me out of all tribulation. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then Saul said to David, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thou, my son David: thou shalt both do great <hi type="italic">things,</hi> and also shalt still prevail. So David went on his way, and Saul returned to his place. <div eID="gen5853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5854" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Saul's penitent confession of his fault and folly in persecuting David and his promise to do so no more. This second instance of David's respect to him wrought more upon him than the former, and extorted from him better acknowledgements, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.21">v. 21</reference>. 1. He owns himself melted and quite overcome by David's kindness to him: "<hi type="italic">My soul was precious in thy eyes this day,</hi> which, I thought, had been odious!" 2. He acknowledges he has done very wrong to persecute him, that he has therein acted against God's law (<hi type="italic">I have sinned</hi>), and against his own interest (<hi type="italic">I have played the fool</hi>), in pursuing him as an enemy who would have been one of his best friends, if he could but have thought so. "Herein (says he) I have <hi type="italic">erred exceedingly,</hi> and wronged both thee and myself." Note, Those that sin play the fool and err exceedingly, those especially that hate and persecute God's people, <reference osisRef="Job.19 Job.28">Job xix. 28</reference>. 3. He invites him to court again: <hi type="italic">Return, my son David.</hi> Those that have understanding will see it to be their interest to have those about them that <hi type="italic">behave themselves wisely,</hi> as David did, and have God with them. 4. He promises him that he will not persecute him as he has done, but protect him: <hi type="italic">I will no more do thee harm.</hi> We have reason to think, according to the mind he was now in, that he meant as he said, and yet neither his confession nor his promise of amendment came from a principle of true repentance. <div eID="gen5854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5855" type="x-p"/> II. David's improvement of Saul's convictions and confessions and the evidence he had to produce of his own sincerity. He desired that one of the footmen might fetch the spear (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.22">v. 22</reference>), and then (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.23">v. 23</reference>), 1. He appeals to God as judge of the controversy: <hi type="italic">The Lord render to every man his righteousness.</hi> David, by faith, is sure that he will do it because he infallibly knows the true characters of all persons and actions and is inflexibly just to render to every man according to his work, and, by prayer, he desires he would do it. Herein he does, in effect, pray against Saul, who had dealt unrighteously and unfaithfully with him (<hi type="italic">Give them according to their deeds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">Ps. xxviii. 4</reference>); but he principally intends it as a prayer for himself, that God would protect him in his righteousness and faithfulness, and also reward him, since Saul so ill requited him. 2. He reminds Saul again of the proof he had now given of his respect to him from a principle of loyalty: <hi type="italic">I would not stretch forth my hand against the Lord's anointed,</hi> intimating to Saul that the anointing oil was his protection, for which he was indebted to the Lord and ought to express his gratitude to him (had he been a common person David would not have been so tender of him), perhaps with this further implication, that Saul knew, or had reason to think, David was the Lord's anointed too, and therefore, by the same rule, Saul ought to be as tender of David's life as David had been of his. 3. Not relying much upon Saul's promises, he puts himself under God's protection and begs his favour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.24">v. 24</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let my life be much set by in the eyes of the Lord,</hi> how light soever thou makest of it." Thus, for his kindness to Saul, he takes God to be his paymaster, which those may with a holy confidence do that <hi type="italic">do well and suffer for it.</hi> <div eID="gen5855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5856" type="x-p"/> III. Saul's prediction of David's advancement. He commends him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be thou, my son David.</hi> So strong was the conviction Saul was now under of David's honesty that he was not ashamed to condemn himself and applaud David, even in the hearing of his own soldiers, who could not but blush to think that they had come out so furiously against a man whom their master, when he meets him, caresses thus. He foretels his victories, and his elevation at last: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt do great things.</hi> Note, Those who make conscience of doing that which is truly good may come, by the divine assistance, to do that which is truly great. He adds, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt also still prevail,</hi> more and more," he means against himself, but is loth to speak that out. The princely qualities which appeared in David—his generosity in sparing Saul, his military authority in reprimanding Abner for sleeping, his care of the public good, and the signal tokens of God's presence with him—convinced Saul that he would certainly be advanced to the throne at last, according to the prophecies concerning him. <div eID="gen5856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5857" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> A palliative cure being thus made of the wound, they parted friends. Saul returned to Gibeah <hi type="italic">re infecta—without accomplishing his design,</hi> and ashamed of the expedition he had made; but David could not take his word so far as to return with him. Those that have once been false are not easily trusted another time. Therefore <hi type="italic">David went on his way.</hi> And, after this parting, it does not appear that ever Saul and David saw one another again.  <chapter eID="1Sam.26"/> <div eID="gen5857" type="x-p"/>

entries.e6f4aa6a1f7f0d1575e23788c954405a559f48c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2777"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <div sID="gen3800" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1-1Sam.26.4">1Sa 26:1-4</reference>. Saul Comes to the Hill of Hachilah against David.<div eID="gen3800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2777"/><hi type="bold">1-2. the Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah--</hi>This people seem to have thought it impossible for David to escape, and therefore recommended themselves to Saul, by giving him secret information (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference>). The knowledge of their treachery makes it appear strange that David should return to his former haunt in their neighborhood; but, perhaps he did it to be near Abigail's possessions, and under the impression that Saul had become mollified. But the king had relapsed into his old enmity. Though Gibeah, as its name imports, stood on an elevated position, and the desert of Ziph, which was in the hilly region of Judea, may have been higher than Gibeah, it was still necessary to descend in leaving the latter place; thence Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.2">1Sa 26:2</reference>) "went down to the wilderness of Ziph." <div eID="gen3801" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5ebe1b03a933849bb779993f02551a679fbe523: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2778"/><div sID="gen3802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2778"/><hi type="bold">4-5. David ... sent out spies ... and David arose, and came to the place where Saul had pitched--</hi>Having obtained certain information of the locality, he seems, accompanied by his nephew (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.6">1Sa 26:6</reference>), to have hid himself, perhaps disguised, in a neighboring wood, or hill, on the skirts of the royal camp towards night, and waited to approach it under covert of the darkness.<div eID="gen3802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3803" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.5-1Sam.26.25">1Sa 26:5-25</reference>. David Stays Abishai from Killing Saul, but Takes His Spear and Cruse. <div eID="gen3803" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2742c8b49de7d58bbff495e1214ba2b7ef5d0ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2780"/><div sID="gen3805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2780"/><hi type="bold">8-12. Then said Abishai to David, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand--</hi>This midnight stratagem shows the activity and heroic enterprise of David's mind, and it was in unison with the style of warfare in ancient times.<div eID="gen3805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let me smite him ... even to the earth at once--</hi>The ferocious vehemence of the speaker is sufficiently apparent from his language, but David's magnanimity soared far above the notions of his followers. Though Saul's cruelty and perfidy and general want of right principle had sunk him to a low pitch of degradation, yet that was no reason for David's imitating him in doing wrong. Besides, he was the sovereign; David was a subject. Though God had rejected him from the kingdom, it was in every way the best and most dutiful course, instead of precipitating his fall by imbruing their hands in his blood and thereby contracting the guilt of a great crime, to wait the awards of that retributive providence which sooner or later would take him off by some sudden and mortal blow. He who, with impetuous haste was going to exterminate Nabal, meekly spared Saul. But Nabal refused to give a tribute to which justice and gratitude, no less than custom, entitled David. Saul was under the judicial infatuation of heaven. Thus David withheld the hand of Abishai; but, at the same time, he directed him to carry off some things which would show where they had been, and what they had done. Thus he obtained the best of victories over him, by heaping coals of fire on his head. <div eID="gen3806" type="x-p"/>
entries.7805f01d3fdaa5b4f77df93347757d8ab39c1e83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2782"/><div sID="gen3809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2782"/><hi type="bold">13-20. Then David ... stood on the top of an hill afar off ... and cried to the people--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Judg.9.7">Jud 9:7</reference>). The extraordinary purity and elasticity of the air in Palestine enable words to be distinctly heard that are addressed by a speaker from the top of one hill to people on that of another, from which it is separated by a deep intervening ravine. Hostile parties can thus speak to each other, while completely beyond the reach of each other's attack. It results from the peculiar features of the country in many of the mountain districts. <div eID="gen3809" type="x-p"/>
entries.1458fe89138edbf1e424863c19bed96f71aedd4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2786"/><div sID="gen3816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2786"/><hi type="bold">25. So David went on his way--</hi>Notwithstanding this sudden relenting of Saul, David placed no confidence in his professions or promises, but wisely kept at a distance and awaited the course of Providence. <chapter eID="1Sam.26"/>

entries.3f5278d6ee12f0cb4bc4bdd7ff4dce309b81cbb2: <div eID="gen10456" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10457" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10458" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10458" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10457" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10459" type="x-p"/> The Ziphites inform Saul of David's hiding place, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">1Sam 26:1</reference>. Saul, with three thousand men, goes in pursuit of him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.2">1Sam 26:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.3">1Sam 26:3</reference>. David sends out spies; and finds where Saul had pitched his camp; and he and Abishai come to the camp by night, find all asleep, and bring away Saul's spear, and the cruse of water that was at his head, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.4-1Sam.26.12">1Sam 26:4-12</reference>. David goes to the opposite hill; awakes Abner, captain of Saul's host; chides him for being so careless of his master's life; and calls on Saul to send one of his servants for the spear; and severely chides him for his continued hostility to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.13-1Sam.26.24">1Sam 26:13-24</reference>. Saul humbles himself to David; promises to persecute him no more; and returns to his own place, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.25">1Sam 26:25</reference>. <div eID="gen10459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10460" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10461" type="x-p"/> The Ziphites came - This is the second time that these enemies of David endeavored to throw him into the hands of Saul. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sam 23:19</reference>.
entries.62ab0d2f951bf176ab29ef05af2421d4415a4a00: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10462" type="x-p"/> Three thousand chosen men - Though they knew that David was but six hundred strong, yet Saul thought it was not safe to pursue such an able general with a less force than that mentioned in the text; and, that he might the better depend on them, they were all elect or picked men out of the whole of his army.
entries.2b42798f1750b9d3cabf7df8a3168ddbe8f8ef98: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10463" type="x-p"/> David arose - As David and his men knew the country, they had many advantages over Saul and his men; and no doubt could often watch them without being discovered. <div eID="gen10463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10464" type="x-p"/> Saul lay in the trench - The word במעגל bammaegal, which we translate in the trench, and in the margin in the midst of his carriages, is rendered by some in a ring of carriages, and by others in the circle, i.e., which was formed by his troops. Luther himself translates it wagenburg, a fortress formed of wagons or carriages. <div eID="gen10464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10465" type="x-p"/> As עגל agal signifies any thing round, it may here refer to a round pavilion or tent made for Saul, or else to the form of his camp. The Arabs, to the present day, always form a circle in their encampments, and put their principal officers in the center.
entries.e9706df28bf8420d8fff5feb6b5e35e6df024529: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10466" type="x-p"/> Abishai the son of Zeruiah - She was David's sister; and therefore Abishai and Joab were nephews to David.
entries.17272e4d2025734d31e762c81aa4a11db941ea6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10467" type="x-p"/> God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand - Here Abishai uses the same language as did David's men, when Saul came into the cave at En-gedi, (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.4">1Sam 24:4</reference>, etc.), and David uses the same language in reply.
entries.d8f448f7b2d2e5c6edc40004f2b0054570b6c0e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10468" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall smite him - He shall die by a stroke of the Divine judgment; or his day shall come to die - he shall die a natural death; which in the course of things must be before mine, and thus I shall get rid of mine enemy; or he shall descend into the battle, and perish - he shall fall by the enemies of his country. These are the three ordinary ways by which man accomplishes, as a hireling, his day. Murder David could not consider to be lawful; this would have been taking the matter out of God's hand, and this David would not do.
entries.7115c451814cca887b16a6ac9fb83100ff1a0fe1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10469" type="x-p"/> David took the spear and the cruse - The spear, we have already seen, was the emblem of power and regal dignity. But it is usual, in Arab camps, for every man to have his lance stuck in the ground beside him, that he may be ready for action in a moment. The cruse of water resembled, in some measure, the canteens of our soldiers. In such a climate, where water was always scarce, it was necessary for each man to carry a little with him, to refresh him on his march. <div eID="gen10469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10470" type="x-p"/> A deep sleep from the Lord - It is the same word which is used, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">Gen 2:21</reference>, to describe the sleep which God caused to fall upon Adam, when he formed Eve out of his side.
entries.7e2152e69d71303d3795513b754c3345e338a11e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10471" type="x-p"/> Art not thou a valiant man? - This is a strong irony. Ye are worthy to die; ye are sons of death - ye deserve death for this neglect of your king. And had not Saul been so deeply affected with David's generosity in preserving his life, he had doubtless put Abner and his chief officers to death; though they were not to blame, as their apparent neglect was the effect of a supernatural sleep.
entries.915f93f5e3a7b5eeea88759884706c4ce1867a1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10472" type="x-p"/> Let him accept an offering - If God have stirred thee up against me, why, then, let him deliver my life into thy hand, and accept it as a sacrifice. But as the word is מנחה minchah, a gratitude-offering, perhaps the sense may be this: Let God accept a gratitude-offering from thee, for having purged the land of a worker of iniquity; for, were I not such, God would never stir thee up against me. <div eID="gen10472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10473" type="x-p"/> But if they be the children of men - If men have, by false representations, lies, and slanders, stirred thee up against an innocent man, then let them be cursed before the Lord. If I am guilty, I deserve to die; if not, those who seek my life should be destroyed. <div eID="gen10473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10474" type="x-p"/> Saying, Go, serve other gods - His being obliged to leave the tabernacle, and the place where the true worship of God was performed, and take refuge among idolaters, said in effect, Go, serve other gods.
entries.ae04f9546757dbbd3d7a334ce8f44ff539b6b298: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10475" type="x-p"/> As when one doth hunt a partridge - It is worthy of remark that the Arabs, observing that partridges, being put up several times, soon become so weary as not to be able to fly; they in this manner hunt them upon the mountains, till at last they can knock them down with their clubs. <div eID="gen10475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10476" type="x-p"/> It was in this manner that Saul hunted David, coming hastily upon him, and putting him up from time to time, in hopes that he should at length, by frequent repetitions of it, be able to destroy him. See Harmer.
entries.079b80a388875393d2c37f2662284dc1be07331c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10477" type="x-p"/> I have sinned - Perhaps the word חטאתי chatathi, "I have sinned," should be read, I have erred, or, have been mistaken. I have taken thee to be a very different man from what I find thee to be. Taken literally it was strictly true. He often purposed the spilling of David's blood; and thus, again and again, sinned against his life.
entries.aea876bae6129430361b86a2219ec2ddc55303ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10478" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt both do great things, and also shalt still prevail. - The Hebrew is גם עשה תעשה וגם יכל תוכל gam asoh thaaseh, vegam yachol tuchal; "Also in doing thou shalt do, and being able thou shalt be able; which the Targum translates, also in reigning thou shalt reign, and in prospering thou shalt prosper; which in all probability is the meaning. <div eID="gen10478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10479" type="x-p"/> There is a vast deal of dignity in this speech of David, arising from a consciousness of his own innocence. He neither begs his life from Saul, nor offers one argument to prevail upon him to desist from his felonious attempts, but refers the whole matter to God, as the judge and vindicator of oppressed innocence. Saul himself is speechless, except in the simple acknowledgment of his sin; and in the behalf of their king not one of his officers has one word to say! It is strange that none of them offered now to injure the person of David; but they saw that he was most evidently under the guardian care of God, and that their master was apparently abandoned by him. Saul invites David to return, but David knew the uncertainty of Saul's character too well to trust himself in the power of this infatuated king. How foolish are the counsels of men against God! When he undertakes to save, who can destroy? And who can deliver out of his hands?  <chapter eID="1Sam.26"/> <div eID="gen10479" type="x-p"/>

entries.00ab7b6b214eb14687f0f2c1b47e0ad3099087b7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1-1Sam.26.2">1Sa 26:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen4125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4126" type="x-p"/> The second betrayal of David by the Ziphites occurred after David had married Abigail at Carmel, and when he had already returned to the desert of Judah. On <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">1Sa 26:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.2">1Sa 26:2</reference> compare the explanations of <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference> and 1Sa 24:3. Instead of “<hi type="italic">before</hi> (in the face of) <hi type="italic">Jeshimon</hi>” (i.e., the wilderness), we find the situation defined more precisely in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference>, as “<hi type="italic">to the right</hi> (i.e., on the south) <hi type="italic">of the wilderness</hi>” (Jeshimon).
entries.1656f35349599ad3a024d9b1b910cd43460f11f9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.3-1Sam.26.4">1Sa 26:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen4126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4127" type="x-p"/> When David saw (i.e., perceived) in the desert that Saul was coming behind him, he sent out spies, and learned from them <hi type="italic">that he certainly had come</hi> (אל־נכון, for a certainty, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.23">1Sa 23:23</reference>).
entries.7e349b00dfb60fcac09ed33f495b9c97c1af0fd7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.5-1Sam.26.7">1Sa 26:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen4127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4128" type="x-p"/> Upon the receipt of this information, David rose up with two attendants (mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.6">1Sa 26:6</reference>) to reconnoitre the camp of Saul. When he saw the place where Saul and his general Abner were lying - Saul was lying <hi type="italic">by the waggon rampart</hi>, and the fighting men were encamped round about him - he said to Ahimelech and Abishai, “<hi type="italic">Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?</hi>” Whereupon Abishai declared himself ready to do so; and they both went by night, and found Saul sleeping with all the people. <hi type="italic">Ahimelech</hi> the Hittite is never mentioned again; but <hi type="italic">Abishai</hi> the son of Zeruiah, David’s sister (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference>), and a brother of Joab, was afterwards a celebrated general of David, as was also his brother Joab (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2Sa 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.2">2Sa 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>). Saul’s spear was <hi type="italic">pressed</hi> (stuck) <hi type="italic">into the ground at his head</hi>, as a sign that the king was sleeping there, for the spear served Saul as a sceptre (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>).
entries.1474d91389cb87d8c643a17b833a0a10fdf1f42c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8-1Sam.26.11">1Sa 26:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen4128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4129" type="x-p"/> When Abishai exclaimed, “<hi type="italic">God hath delivered thine enemy into thy hand: now will I pierce him with the spear into the ground with a stroke, and will give no second</hi>” (sc., stroke: the Vulgate rendering gives the sense exactly: et secundo non opus erit, there will be no necessity for a second), David replied, “Destroy him not; for who hath stretched out his hand against the anointed of the Lord, and remained unhurt?” נקּה, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.19">Exo 21:19</reference>; Num 5:31. He then continued (in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">1Sa 26:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.11">1Sa 26:11</reference>): “As truly as Jehovah liveth, unless Jehovah smite him (i.e., carry him off with a stroke; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.38">1Sa 25:38</reference>), or his day cometh that he dies (i.e., or he dies a natural death; 'his day' denoting the day of death, as in <reference osisRef="Job.14.6">Job 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">Job 15:32</reference>), or he goes into battle and is carried off, far be it from me with Jehovah (מיהוה, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.7">1Sa 24:7</reference>) to stretch forth my hand against Jehovah’s anointed.” The apodosis to <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">1Sa 26:10</reference> commences with חלילה, “far be it,” or “the Lord forbid,” in 1Sa 26:11. “Take now the spear which is at his head, and the pitcher, and let us go.”
entries.941368eb09c3a82681e9a4a8580a68b4a9d74749: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.12">1Sa 26:12</reference> <div eID="gen4129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4130" type="x-p"/> They departed with these trophies, without any one waking up and seeing them, because they were all asleep, as a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them. שׁאוּל מראשׁתי stands for שׁ ממראשׁתי, “from the head of Saul,” with מ dropped. The expression “<hi type="italic">a deep sleep of Jehovah</hi>,” i.e., a deep sleep sent or inflicted by Jehovah, points to the fact that the Lord favoured David’s enterprise.
entries.e8885babbcb100db026bd58e221e7b28d9871051: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.13">1Sa 26:13</reference> <div eID="gen4130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4131" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And David went over to the other side, and placed himself upon the top of the mountain afar off</hi> (the space between them was great), <hi type="italic">and cried to the people</hi>,” etc. Saul had probably encamped with his fighting men on the slope of the ill Hachilah, so that a valley separated him from the opposite hill, from which David had no doubt reconnoitred the camp and then gone down to it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.6">1Sa 26:6</reference>), and to which he returned after the deed was accomplished. The statement that this mountain was far off, so that there was a great space between David and Saul, not only favours the accuracy of the historical tradition, but shows that David reckoned far less now upon any change in the state of Saul’s mind than he had done before, when he followed Saul without hesitation from the cave and called after him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.9">1Sa 24:9</reference>), and that in fact he rather feared lest Saul should endeavour to get him into his power as soon as he woke from his sleep.
entries.44acea033a7e80ab4bd531a771bb65481fef7e9f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.14">1Sa 26:14</reference> <div eID="gen4131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> David called out to Abner, whose duty it was as general to defend the life of his king. And Abner replied, “<hi type="italic">Who art thou, who criest out to the king?</hi>” i.e., offendest the king by thy shouting, and disturbest his rest.
entries.da90a9b188c8d21ae20897dfe322479635b46e9d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.15-1Sam.26.16">1Sa 26:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4133" type="x-p"/> David in return taunted Abner with having watched the king carelessly, and made himself chargeable with his death. “<hi type="italic">For one of the people came to destroy thy lord the king</hi>.” As a proof of this, he then showed him the spear and pitcher that he had taken away with him. ראה is to be repeated in thought before את־צפּחת: “<hi type="italic">look where the king’s spear is; and</hi> (look) <hi type="italic">at the pitcher at his head</hi>,” sc., where it is. These reproaches that were cast at Abner were intended to show to Saul, who might at any rate possibly hear, and in fact did hear, that David was the most faithful defender of his life, more faithful than his closest and most zealous servants.
entries.18dcbca1de26b67448414f93eb61ade62bf903e9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.17-1Sam.26.19">1Sa 26:17-19</reference> <div eID="gen4133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4134" type="x-p"/> When Saul heard David’s voice (for he could hardly have seen David, as the occurrence took place before daybreak, at the latest when the day began to dawn), and David had made himself known to the king in reply to his inquiry, David said, “<hi type="italic">Why doth my lord pursue his servant? for what have I done, and what evil is in my hand?</hi>” He then gave him the well-meant advice, to seek reconciliation for his wrath against him, and not to bring upon himself the guilt of allowing David to find his death in a foreign land. The words, “<hi type="italic">and now let my lord the king hear the saying of his servant</hi>,” serve to indicate that what follows is important, and worthy of laying to heart. In his words, David supposes two cases as conceivable causes of Saul’s hostility: (1) if Jehovah hath stirred thee up against me; (2) if men have done so. In the first case, he proposes as the best means of overcoming this instigation, that He (Jehovah) should smell an offering. The <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> ירח only means to smell, not to cause to smell. The subject is Jehovah. Smelling a sacrifice is an anthropomorphic term, used to denote the divine satisfaction (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen 8:21</reference>). The meaning of the words, “<hi type="italic">let Jehovah smell sacrifice</hi>,” is therefore, “let Saul appease the wrath of God by the presentation of acceptable sacrifices.” What sacrifices they are which please God, is shown in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18-Ps.51.19">Psa 51:18-19</reference>; and it is certainly not by accident merely that David uses the word <hi type="italic">minchah</hi>, the technical expression in the law for the bloodless sacrifice, which sets forth the sanctification of life in good works. The thought to which David gives utterance here, namely, that God instigates a man to evil actions, is met with in other passages of the Old Testament. It not only lies at the foundation of the words of David in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Psa 51:6</reference> (cf. Hengstenberg on <hi type="italic">Psalms</hi>), but is also clearly expressed in <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.1">2Sa 24:1</reference>, where Jehovah instigates David to number the people, and where this instigation is described as a manifestation of the anger of God against Israel; and in 2Sa 16:10., where David says, with regard to Shimei, that God had bade him curse him. These passages also show that God only instigates those who have sinned against Him to evil deeds; and therefore that the instigation consists in the fact that God impels sinners to manifest the wickedness of their hearts in deeds, or furnishes the opportunity and occasion for the unfolding and practical manifestation of the evil desire of the heart, that the sinner may either be brought to the knowledge of his more evil ways and also to repentance, through the evil deed and its consequences, or, if the heart should be hardened still more by the evil deed, that it may become ripe for the judgment of death. The instigation of a sinner to evil is simply one peculiar way in which God, as a general rule, punishes sins through sinners; for God only instigates to evil actions such as have drawn down the wrath of God upon themselves in consequence of their sin. When David supposes the fact that Jehovah has instigated Saul against him, he acknowledges, implicitly at least, that he himself is a sinner, whom the Lord may be intending to punish, though without lessening Saul’s wrong by this indirect confession. <div eID="gen4134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> The second supposition is: “<hi type="italic">if, however, children of men</hi>” (sc., have instigated thee against me); in which case “<hi type="italic">let them be cursed before the Lord; for they drive me now</hi> (this day) <hi type="italic">that I dare not attach myself to the inheritance of Jehovah</hi> (i.e., the people of God), <hi type="italic">saying, Go, serve other gods</hi>.” The meaning is this: They have carried it so far now, that I am obliged to separate from the people of God, to fly from the land of the Lord, and, because far away from His sanctuary, to serve other gods. The idea implied in the closing words was, that Jehovah could only be worshipped in Canaan, at the sanctuary consecrated to Him, because it was only there that He manifested himself to His people, and revealed His face or gracious presence (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.42.2-Ps.42.3">Psa 42:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Psa 84:11</reference>; Psa 143:6.). “We are not to understand that the enemies of David were actually accustomed to use these very words, but David was thinking of deeds rather than words” (Calvin).
entries.19cdbc3ab5f327b0a909477fbb3a34ce7613d5f4: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">1Sa 26:20</reference> <div eID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4136" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now let not my blood fall to the earth far away from the face of the Lord</hi>,” i.e., do not carry it so far as to compel me to perish in a foreign land. “<hi type="italic">For the king of Israel has gone out to seek a single flea </hi>(vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.15">1Sa 24:15</reference>), <hi type="italic">as one hunts a partridge upon the mountains</hi>.” This last comparison does not of course refer to the first, so that “the object of comparison is compared again with something else,” as Thenius supposes, but it refers rather to the whole of the previous clause. The king of Israel is pursuing something very trivial, and altogether unworthy of his pursuit, just as if one were hunting a partridge upon the mountains. “No one would think it worth his while to hunt a single partridge that had flown to the mountains, when they may be found in coveys in the fields” (Winer, Bibl. R. W. ii. p. 307). This comparison, therefore, does not presuppose that קרא must be a bird living upon the mountains, as Thenius maintains, so as to justify his altering the text according to the Septuagint. These words of David were perfectly well adapted to sharpen Saul’s conscience, and induce him to desist from his enmity, if he still had an ear for the voice of truth.
entries.08892360d38e149168d1d89a6f0cfe20b18ce529: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.21">1Sa 26:21</reference> <div eID="gen4136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4137" type="x-p"/> Moreover, Saul could not help confessing, “<hi type="italic">I have sinned: return, my son David; I will do thee harm no more, because my life was precious in thine eyes that day</hi>.” A good intention, which he never carried out. “He declared that he would never do any more what he had already so often promised not to do again; and yet he did not fail to do it again and again. He ought rather to have taken refuge with God, and appealed to Him for grace, that he might not fall into such sins again; yea, he should have entreated David himself to pray for him” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>). He adds still further, “<hi type="italic">Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have gone sore astray</hi>;” but yet he persists in this folly. “There is no sinner so hardened, but that God gives him now and then some rays of light, which show him all his error. But, alas! when they are awakened by such divine movings, it is only for a few moments; and such impulses are no sooner past, than they fall back again immediately into their former life, and forget all that they have promised.”
entries.c7eb1dc5de6a0522dbdfc61268bce642836bd001: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.22-1Sam.26.23">1Sa 26:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen4137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4138" type="x-p"/> David then bade the king send a servant to fetch back the spear and pitcher, and reminded him again of the recompense of God: “<hi type="italic">Jehovah will recompense His righteousness and His faithfulness to the man into whose hand Jehovah hath given thee to-day; and</hi> (for) <hi type="italic">I would not stretch out my hand against the anointed of the Lord</hi>.”
entries.4530b5d32e2a587a893ad99e1340292ea16be82c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.24-1Sam.26.25">1Sa 26:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen4138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4139" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Behold, as thy soul has been greatly esteemed in my eyes to-day, so will my soul be greatly esteemed in the eyes of Jehovah, that He will save me out of all tribulation</hi>.” These words do not contain any “sounding of his own praises” (Thenius), but are merely the testimony of a good conscience before God in the presence of an enemy, who is indeed obliged to confess his wrong-doing, but who no longer feels or acknowledges his need of forgiveness. For even Saul’s reply to these words in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.25">1Sa 26:25</reference> (“Blessed art thou, my son David: thou wilt undertake, and also prevail:” תּוּכל יכל, lit. to vanquish, i.e., to carry out what one undertakes) does not express any genuine goodwill towards David, but only an acknowledgment, forced upon him by this fresh experience of David’s magnanimity, that God was blessing all his undertakings, so that he would prevail. Saul had no more thoughts of any real reconciliation with David. “David went his way, and Saul turned to his place” (cf. Num 24:25). Thus they parted, and never saw each other again. There is nothing said about Saul returning to his house, as there was when his life was first spared (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">1Sa 24:22</reference>). On the contrary, he does not seem to have given up pursuing David; for, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:1-12</reference>, David was obliged to take refuge in a foreign land, and carry out what he had described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1Sa 26:19</reference> as his greatest calamity. David at Ziklag in the Land of the Philistines - <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:1-12</reference> <div eID="gen4139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4140" type="x-p"/> In his despair of being able permanently to escape the plots of Saul in the land of Israel, David betook himself, with his attendants, to the neighbouring land of the Philistines, to king Achish of Gath, and received from him the town of Ziklag, which was assigned him at his own request as a dwelling-place (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:1-7</reference>). From this point he made attacks upon certain tribes on the southern frontier of Canaan which were hostile to Israel, but described them to Achish as attacks upon Judah and its dependencies, that he might still retain the protection of the Philistian chief (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8-1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:8-12</reference>). David had fled to Achish at Gath once before; but on that occasion he had been obliged to feign insanity in order to preserve his life, because he was recognised as the conqueror of Goliath. This act of David was not forgotten by the Philistines even now. But as David had been pursued by Saul for many years, Achish did not hesitate to give a place of refuge in his land to the fugitive who had been outlawed by the king of Israel, the arch-enemy of the Philistines, possibly with the hope that if a fresh war with Saul should break out, he should be able to reap some advantage from David’s friendship.  <chapter eID="1Sam.26"/> <div eID="gen4140" type="x-p"/>
